How long someone must occupy land to claim it

Connecticut's limit is fifteen years, and the statute speaks from the owner's side. Section 52-575(a) says no one may enter lands except within fifteen years after the right or title first accrues, or within fifteen years after being ousted from possession. It tells an owner how long the right to take land back lasts and what the owner can do to stop the clock.

A claimant would also have to prove more than time in the house, and an attorney's read of your facts matters more than any short summary. Fifteen years is the number to remember. Nothing in section 52-575 shortens it for an occupant who has been inside only a short while.

How an owner can interrupt the clock

Serve a written notice, record it, then file suit within one year. Under section 52-575(a), entry is not enough on its own. Within the fifteen-year period, a person claiming ownership must give written notice to those in possession saying they dispute the right of possession and want to keep the other party from acquiring it.

The notice must be served and recorded as sections 47-39 and 47-40 provide, and it counts as an interruption of use and possession. The owner must then start a court action within one year after the notice is recorded.

  • Write a notice stating that you dispute the right of possession.
  • Serve it like an original summons, as section 47-39 directs.
  • Record it on the land records in the town where the land lies.
  • Start the court action within one year after recording.

Section 47-39 allows service on a tenant or occupant of the estate for a person outside the state, or failing that, posting a copy on the house or another conspicuous part of the premises. Section 47-40 handles the case of an unknown party. Service rules are technical, so have a lawyer review the paperwork.

Minors, prisoners and people lacking capacity

The time limits stretch a little for them. Under section 52-575(b), someone with a right of entry who was a minor, non compos mentis or imprisoned when the right first accrued, along with that person's heirs, may enter and serve and record notice within five years after reaching full age, regaining sound mind or being released.

This shows up in family houses. A property inherited by an heir who was a child at the owner's death, or a co-owner who spent years incarcerated, may carry a longer window than the fifteen-year headline suggests. The statute also holds that the limit does not begin to run against an owner of a remainder or reversionary interest until the preceding particular estate ends.

So when ownership history is tangled, don't assume the clock ran out on the owner. Pull the chain of title and ask a lawyer to read it.

Someone is living in my house and I never rented to them

Section 47a-23 speaks to this directly. An owner may serve a notice to quit when the premises are occupied by someone who never had a right or privilege to occupy them, and also when someone had that right at first but it has ended.

The notice to quit must be in writing, in the form the statute supplies, and given at least three days before the time stated for the occupant to leave. If the occupant stays, the next step is a summary process case in court. Changing locks or removing belongings is not the next step.

SituationStatute and step
Occupant never had any right to be there47a-23(a)(2), notice to quit
Right to occupy existed but ended47a-23(a)(3), notice to quit
Lease ended or rent not paid47a-23(a)(1), notice to quit
Owner wants to stop an adverse claim running52-575(a), notice served and recorded, suit within one year

Squatter or tenant?

A tenant came in under a rental agreement or lease, written or oral. A squatter did not. That split decides which part of section 47a-23 applies. Item (1) covers leases and rental agreements that end by lapse of time, by an expressed stipulation, for violation, or for nonpayment of rent. Items (2) and (3) cover occupants who never had a right or whose right has ended.

Work out which one you have before writing a notice. A person paying rent in cash, or a relative who stayed on after a death, may be treated differently from a stranger who broke in. Text messages, receipts and a written history help. Our Connecticut landlord and tenant page goes into rental occupants in more detail.

Recorded deeds and adverse claims

Recording a deed is separate from the notice that interrupts an adverse claim. Section 47-10 makes a conveyance ineffective against anyone but the grantor and heirs unless it is recorded in the town where the land lies, so a buyer should always record. The method for interrupting a claim is the recorded notice described in section 52-575(a).

Each of Connecticut's 169 municipalities keeps its own land records. Owners of vacant property can visit regularly and keep dated photographs of its condition and any signs that someone has moved in.

Selling a house with an occupant who will not leave

You can, though it narrows the buyer pool. Anyone needing a mortgage may struggle to close, because possession on closing day is uncertain. Investors who buy as-is sometimes can, but the occupancy will move the price and the timing, and an attorney should read any contract that depends on the occupant leaving.

Before you list, gather what you can: the deed, tax bills, any notice to quit with proof of service, and a note of when you last controlled the property. That file speeds the title search and shows a buyer what is left to do.

Records to keep on vacant or inherited property

Every deadline in this area runs from a date you may later have to prove, so keep a short paper trail. Recording, service and filing each leave a record.

  • The recorded deed, with the town clerk's recording information.
  • Any notice served under section 52-575, with the proof of service and the recording receipt.
  • The date a notice to quit was given under section 47a-23, and the date stated in it.
  • Dated photographs of the property, taken on each visit.
  • Property tax bills, which show who the town treats as owner.

The clerk in the town where the house sits is the right office to ask what is recorded against it.

Frequently asked questions

Can a squatter take ownership of a Connecticut house?

Only if every requirement of adverse possession is met for the full period. Section 52-575 sets a fifteen-year limit on the owner's right to enter, and an attorney should assess the facts.

How many years does adverse possession take in Connecticut?

Fifteen years is the period in section 52-575(a). Longer periods can apply when the owner was a minor, of unsound mind or imprisoned when the right first accrued.

How do I stop someone from claiming my land?

Serve written notice disputing their right of possession, record it as sections 47-39 and 47-40 direct, and begin an action within one year after recording.

What notice do I give someone who never had permission to stay?

A written notice to quit under section 47a-23, given at least three days before the date stated for the occupant to leave. If they stay, a summary process action follows.

Can I sell my house while a squatter is inside?

You can, but financed buyers may struggle to close. An as-is cash buyer may, and the occupancy affects price and timing.

Connecticut landlord and tenant laws by chapter

Most landlord and tenant rules live in Title 47a of the General Statutes, split into chapters by subject. A landlord preparing to sell a rental will touch several of them, so it helps to know which chapter answers which question.

ChapterSubject
830Rights and responsibilities of landlord and tenant
831Security deposits
832Summary process (eviction)
833Entry and detainer
833aPublic enforcement of health and safety standards in rented dwellings

The Judicial Branch law library keeps a landlord and tenant page with links to these chapters, to forms, and to research reports from the Office of Legislative Research. Treat it as a place to start research, not as legal advice.

What a landlord must keep in working order

Under section 47a-7, a landlord has to follow the building and housing codes that affect health and safety and keep the premises fit and habitable. The duty has exceptions when the tenant or a guest made the place unfit on purpose. The statute spells out the day-to-day tasks.

  • Make repairs and do whatever is needed to keep the premises fit and habitable.
  • Keep the common areas clean and safe.
  • Keep electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating and ventilating systems, appliances and elevators that the landlord supplies or must supply in good and safe working order.
  • Provide and maintain containers for ashes, garbage and other waste.

These duties follow the house. A buyer who steps into the landlord's role inherits them, and an inspection that turns up tired heating or plumbing in a rented unit can pull an offer down. Investors buying as-is usually price that risk in instead of asking for repairs.

Late rent and late fees

Rent is not late for nine days after the due date, or four days on a one-week tenancy. Only once that grace period ends may a landlord terminate for nonpayment under sections 47a-23 to 47a-23b. The grace rule is section 47a-15a.

A valid written late-charge agreement in the lease lets the landlord charge a fee on a payment made after the grace period. The fee cannot exceed the lesser of five dollars a day, up to fifty dollars, or five percent of the late payment. When a government or charitable entity covers part of the rent, the five percent applies to the tenant's share only. One late payment can carry only one late fee, however long it stays open.

A buyer will want a rent roll and payment history. Clean records of due dates, grace periods and fees head off questions at the closing table.

Showing a rented home to buyers

A landlord can show a rental, within limits. Section 47a-16 says a tenant may not unreasonably refuse consent for the landlord to enter to show the unit to prospective or actual purchasers, in addition to entering to inspect or make repairs.

The tenant's privacy stays protected. Without consent, a landlord may enter only in an emergency (section 47a-16a), under a court order, or when the tenant has abandoned the premises. Entry cannot be abused or used to harass, and it must happen at reasonable times except in an emergency.

Showings go better when planned with the tenant. Set windows and a short list of expected visitors beat a string of last-minute requests. A cash buyer who wants to see a tenant-occupied house can often manage one visit instead of a run of open houses.

Security deposits when the landlord sells

The deposit goes to the new owner. Section 47a-21 treats any voluntary or involuntary transfer of the landlord's interest in residential property as an assignment to the successor of the landlord's security interest in every deposit the tenants paid.

The seller has to move the money. On a transfer from a landlord, other than a receiver, the landlord must withdraw the full deposits plus accrued interest from the escrow account and deliver them to the successor. Where the account also holds deposits for other properties and has less than the total, the seller delivers a pro rata share for the property being sold. A successor includes anyone who gets the landlord's interest by purchase, foreclosure or otherwise.

  • Return deadline: no later than twenty-one days after the tenancy ends, or fifteen days after the tenant gives a written forwarding address, whichever is later.
  • Amount returned: the full deposit plus accrued interest, less any damage deductions the landlord may take.

Notice to tenants after closing

Section 47a-6 requires a landlord, or a successor landlord, to tell the tenant in writing at the time of succession the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises. The statute names a second person too, so read the full text.

The Department of Housing posts mandatory landlord and tenant notice forms on its website, and the Judicial Branch page links to them. A buyer taking over a rental should bring the notice to closing, along with lease copies, the deposit transfer and any records of repairs or complaints.

Tenants take a sale better when they hear about it from the owner. One short written note naming the seller, the buyer and the new contact cuts confusion and missed rent.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Connecticut houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Tenants with extra protection from eviction

Section 47a-23c limits evictions of older and disabled tenants in larger properties. It reaches a tenant who is 62 or older or has a qualifying disability and lives in a building or complex of five or more dwelling units, or in a mobile manufactured home park. Some tenants who live with a relative meeting those conditions are covered as well.

A landlord can sue such a tenant only on the listed grounds, and a rent increase must be fair and equitable under the criteria in section 7-148c. A protected tenant aggrieved by a proposed increase can go to the town's fair rent commission if there is one, or to Superior Court if there is not. Public Act 22-30, which concerns fair rent commissions, took effect October 1, 2022.

Selling the building is not a listed ground. Buyers of small apartment buildings should ask for each tenant's age and status before agreeing on a price.

Before selling a Connecticut rental

Gather the paper trail first. This short list keeps a sale on schedule.

  1. Copy each lease and rental agreement, with rent amounts and dates.
  2. Confirm where each security deposit is held and how much interest has built up.
  3. Write down repair requests and what was done about them under section 47a-7.
  4. Check whether any tenant falls under section 47a-23c.
  5. Decide whether to sell with tenants in place or after they leave, and put any move-out deal in writing.

Landlords with worn-out rentals often sell to a cash investor. The buyer takes the property as-is and deals with the leases after closing, so the owner skips repairs, showings and a lender's approval wait.

Leases and the buyer after closing

A lease does not vanish at closing. Whether it continues depends on its terms and on the notice and court rules, so read it before you set a price and ask an attorney about anything unusual. The buyer becomes the landlord for deposit purposes, takes on the repair duties from section 47a-7, and has to send the written notice about who manages the property.

If the seller and buyer want the unit empty, the only lawful routes are a negotiated move-out agreed in writing or a notice to quit and the court process. A buyer who wants a tenant gone should say so up front, because it changes the price and the closing date.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the maximum security deposit in Connecticut?

The cap is two months' rent for a tenant under 62 and one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older under section 47a-21.

How soon must a landlord return a deposit?

A landlord must deliver the deposit with accrued interest, less allowed deductions, no later than 21 days after the tenancy ends or 15 days after a written forwarding address, whichever is later.

Does a new owner have to honor the existing lease?

The chapter treats a successor as a landlord and passes the deposits along. Whether a lease continues depends on its terms and on the notice and court rules, so read the lease and ask an attorney.

Can a landlord enter a rental without notice?

Only in an emergency, under a court order, as permitted by section 47a-16a, or when the unit has been abandoned. Otherwise entry needs the tenant's consent and a reasonable time.

Where can I find Connecticut landlord and tenant forms?

The Judicial Branch law library page for landlord and tenant law links housing forms, and the Department of Housing posts mandatory notice forms and a model lease.
